Estimating Intrinsic Dimension with MPCurver

Source: vignettes/intrinsic_dimension.Rmd
intrinsic_dimension.Rmd

When the intrinsic dimension is unknown, start with fit_mpcurve(X, intrinsic_dim = "auto") and its default adaptive partition prior. This is computationally simpler than fitting a sequence of candidate dimensions: feature similarity chooses an initial dimension, then one adaptive fit estimates ordering weights and removes numerical-zero orderings.

Use select_mpcurve_dimension() when your analysis calls for explicit model comparison under a fixed uniform feature-assignment prior. The two approaches use different priors and selection rules and can produce different dimensions. Supplying an integer intrinsic_dim = M instead fits that specified dimension. This tutorial shows both estimation approaches; Multiple orderings introduces the model and software use. The algorithm details are available separately.

Example data

We simulate 200 samples and twelve features, with two groups following different latent orderings. The generating dimension is two; it is not supplied to either fitting procedure below.

library(MPCurver)
sim <- simulate_dual_trajectory(
  n = 200,
  d1 = 6,
  d2 = 6,
  d_noise = 0,
  noise_sd = 0.05,
  trajectory_family = c("quadratic", "monotone"),
  seed = 1
)
X <- sim$X

Automatic initialization and adaptive fitting

Use intrinsic_dim = "auto" to choose the starting model dimension from the feature-similarity tree. max_intrinsic_dim bounds the candidate dimensions; here we consider at most four orderings and use twenty position bins. The default adaptive feature-assignment prior is used during fitting.

fit_auto <- fit_mpcurve(
  X,
  intrinsic_dim = "auto",
  num_bins = 20,
  max_iter = 200,
  init_control = mpcurve_init_control(max_intrinsic_dim = 4)
)

Automatic initialization uses spline-R-squared feature similarity by default. It evaluates hierarchical-clustering cuts and selects the eligible cut with the largest mean silhouette. Every cluster must contain at least init_control$min_cluster_size features (default 2). If no multi-ordering cut satisfies this rule, it fits one ordering.

For cluster sizes P_1,\ldots,P_M, the adaptive fit initializes the ordering prior weights as \omega_m=P_m/P, where P is the total number of features. Every feature starts from this same probability vector. After fitting, orderings with numerical-zero estimated prior weights are removed. The returned model contains the estimated number of orderings.

The minimum cluster size prevents a singleton feature from serving as the sole evidence for a latent ordering: sorting that feature by its own values would produce a smooth trajectory by construction. A singleton can reflect noise, weak measurement, or model mismatch; MPCurver has no separate background-feature component.

Inspect the estimated model

fit_auto$intrinsic_dim is the number of orderings in the returned model. Table 1 reports this estimated dimension.

Table 1. Estimated intrinsic dimension of the returned model.
Quantity Field Value
Estimated intrinsic dimension intrinsic_dim 3

For ordering m, empirical Bayes estimates its prior weight as

\widehat\omega_m=\frac{1}{P}\sum_{j=1}^{P} q(Z_j=m),

where P is the number of features. Automatic adaptive fitting removes an ordering when \widehat\omega_m is at or below control$effective_count_tol / P. The tolerance defaults to 1e-8 and identifies estimated prior weights that are numerically close to zero. Automatic adaptive pruning warns when the tolerance exceeds 1e-6, before division by P, because large values may remove supported orderings.

Empty orderings are removed without further fitting. The remaining assignment probabilities and prior weights are normalized, and the final objective is recomputed. Initial dimensions and any removed orderings are recorded in fit_auto$dimension_estimation.

Table 2 shows the estimated prior weights and their corresponding expected feature counts, P\widehat\omega_m.

feature_counts <- colSums(fitted_assignments(fit_auto))
# At the adaptive update, the estimated prior weight equals the mean
# posterior assignment probability; this also covers a single retained ordering.
prior_weights <- colMeans(fitted_assignments(fit_auto))
Table 2. Estimated ordering prior weights and corresponding expected feature counts.
Ordering Prior_weight Expected_feature_count
A 0.50 6
B 0.25 3
C 0.25 3

Use fitted_positions(), fitted_trajectories(), and fitted_assignments() to extract results with consistent dimensions even when the estimated dimension is one. Supplying an integer intrinsic_dim retains that specified dimension. With a fixed feature-assignment prior, automatic fitting retains the dimension chosen at initialization.

Compare dimensions under a uniform prior

select_mpcurve_dimension() fits adjacent model dimensions with a fixed uniform feature-assignment prior and compares final soft-assignment objectives at T=1. Forward selection starts at M=1 and accepts the next dimension only when its objective is strictly larger. Backward selection starts at max_intrinsic_dim and tests smaller dimensions by the same rule.

selected <- select_mpcurve_dimension(
  X,
  max_intrinsic_dim = 4,
  direction = "forward",
  num_bins = 20,
  max_iter = 200
)
selected$intrinsic_dim
#> [1] 2

Each candidate M is fitted once. For M > 1, features are grouped by similarity, and the selected initial_method initializes each group. All candidates use a common grid size and the supplied model and fitting settings. With uniform prior weights, an ordering receiving no feature mass still changes the assignment-prior term by P\log\{M/(M-1)\} relative to the smaller model.

Table 3 records the objective comparisons, including the rejected stopping step when present. Table 4 reports each attempted fit and its convergence status.

selected$dimension_selection$history
Table 3. Adjacent-dimension objective comparisons in forward selection.
From M To M Current objective Candidate objective Change Accepted
1 2 1179.850 2353.147 1173.297 TRUE
2 3 2353.147 2136.357 -216.789 FALSE 
selected$dimension_selection$candidates
Table 4. Initialization, fitting objective, and convergence status for each candidate dimension.
M Initialization Status Objective Converged
1 single success 1179.850 TRUE
2 similarity success 2353.147 TRUE
3 similarity success 2136.357 FALSE

The complete candidate record also contains warnings and errors. Greedy selection depends on initialization and convergence and can stop at a local choice. Inspect these records and, for candidates that reach their iteration limit, increase max_iter before relying on the comparison. The adaptive occupancy count and uniform-prior search use different criteria.
